expect.statement: In observational studies, mostly cross-sectional and mostly in treatment, psychiatric, emergency or criminal-justice samples in which the comparison group often also used other drugs, people with an amphetamine use disorder (amphetamine or methamphetamine) had higher odds of psychosis than people without one: odds ratio 2.4 (95% CI 1.6–3.5; 4 studies, I² 35%) in studies that adjusted for some combination of demographics, other substance use and premorbid risk. The review grades this estimate at its lowest level of evidence (cross-sectional associations within samples of people who use drugs); its four studies were of young offenders, people in methamphetamine rehabilitation, people using methamphetamine at least monthly, and people released from prison (a cohort): in two of them everyone used methamphetamine, so the comparison was with methamphetamine use without a use disorder, and for the prison cohort the review reports no significant relation with later primary psychosis (later substance-induced psychosis was raised). Unadjusted estimates were 3.0 (1.9–4.8; 13 studies, I² 90%) for use disorder and 2.0 (1.3–3.3; 7 studies, I² 80%) for any use; the review's authors consider unadjusted estimates likely inflated by co-occurring risk factors, and comparisons made within samples of people who use other drugs likely to understate the difference from the general population. In post hoc subgroups the association was stronger for psychotic symptoms than for diagnosed psychotic disorders; for any use, the association with a diagnosed disorder was not statistically clear (1.3, 1.0–1.9). Most studies cannot show whether use preceded psychosis. In a general-population birth cohort in Christchurch, New Zealand (962 to 1,025 people at each of five interviews from age 18 to 35), use of methamphetamine or other amphetamine-type stimulants since the previous interview went with reporting at least one psychotic symptom at the same interview (symptoms over the past month at ages 18, 21 and 25, since the previous interview at 30 and 35): odds ratio 1.88 (95% CI 1.55–2.30) unadjusted and 1.33 (1.03–1.72) after adjustment for childhood, family and adolescent factors and for concurrent cannabis use, alcohol use disorder, depression, anxiety and life stress; the outcome was self-reported psychotic experiences on checklist and interview items (35–42% of the cohort reported at least one in each period to age 25), not diagnosed psychosis, and use and symptoms were reported at the same interviews, so this cohort cannot show which came first either. The higher odds were concentrated in the 5% who had ever used at least weekly (2.85, 1.21–6.69, adjusted for childhood, family and adolescent factors only, not for concurrent cannabis use; about 1.3 and not statistically significant for less frequent use). No threshold level of use could be estimated; more frequent use went with more psychotic symptoms in 4 of the 8 study populations that examined it; the systematic review that counted them judged the studies finding this to be of higher quality and rated the evidence on frequency moderate, the only risk factor it rated above low.
expect.plain: In studies mostly in treatment, hospitals or prisons, a meth or amphetamine use disorder went with about two and a half times the odds of psychosis, allowing for some other differences. A study following about 1,000 New Zealanders from birth found any use went with slightly more self-reported psychotic experiences, mostly in people who had ever used at least weekly. Neither settles which came first.
expect.magnitude: Use disorder, adjusted: OR 2.4 (1.6–3.5), 4 studies, n=7648, I² 35%. Unadjusted: use disorder 3.0 (1.9–4.8), 13 studies, n=81,316, I² 90%; any use 2.0 (1.3–3.3), 7 studies, n=3436, I² 80%. Post hoc subgroups (use disorder): psychotic symptoms 4.3 (2.9–6.5) vs diagnosed disorder 2.3 (1.2–4.7). No absolute risks reported. General-population birth cohort (New Zealand): any use since the previous interview, symptoms at the same interview, OR 1.33 (1.03–1.72) after adjustment for fixed and time-varying factors (unadjusted 1.88, 1.55–2.30); ever at least weekly use 2.85 (1.21–6.69), adjusted for fixed factors only; population attributable fraction 8.0% (2.2–14.7%) if causal.
expect.grade.reasoning: Observational, mostly cross-sectional; starts low. The claim is an association and rests on the adjusted use-disorder estimate (2.4, 1.6–3.5; 4 studies, I² 35%); the unadjusted estimates are context, labelled as likely inflated. Risk of bias not downgraded: the adjusted studies accounted for some combination of demographics, other substance use and premorbid risk, the adjusted pool's weighted quality score is 88% in the review, and comparison groups mostly also used other drugs (in two of the four adjusted studies, methamphetamine without a use disorder), which the authors argue makes estimates understate the difference from the general population; residual confounding by unmeasured premorbid factors (family history of psychosis, childhood trauma) remains and is why the claim is worded as an association. Inconsistency not downgraded for the adjusted estimate; the unadjusted estimates are heterogeneous (I² 80–90%). Publication bias could not be assessed (too few studies; AMSTAR 2 critically low); not downgraded, noted. Not upgraded for dose–response: frequency was associated in 4 of 8 populations (evidence the risk-factor review rates moderate), but across different studies and measures rather than as a gradient within one body of evidence; the within-person gradient is rated in the claim on frequency of use within the same people (section 9). McKetin et al. (2013), rated separately in that claim, is inside the unadjusted any-use estimate and is the review's only adjusted any-use estimate (5.3); it is not in the adjusted use-disorder estimate on which this claim rests. Boden et al. (2023), a general-population birth cohort read in full (ROBINS-E high on the first reading, from concerns in several domains), agrees in direction and is smaller after fuller adjustment (any use, OR 1.33, 1.03–1.72, after adjusting for concurrent cannabis use and other time-varying factors; 1.88 unadjusted), which fits the meta-analysis authors' view that unadjusted estimates are inflated; it is not counted as inconsistency, because exposure (any use rather than use disorder), population and outcome (self-reported psychotic experiences) differ. Not upgraded for dose–response: its gradient (2.85 for ever at least weekly use against about 1.3, not significant, for less frequent use) is adjusted only for fixed confounders, is not monotonic (1.37, 1.32, 2.85) and rests on 51 people in the top category. It is an independent sample, though it shares an author with McKetin et al. (2013) and the meta-analysis. Huang et al. (2022), a ten-year retrospective cohort identified by the currency check of 2026-10-16, has not yet been read (built-in browser unavailable on 2026-10-17).

The hazard ratio is adjusted only for age, sex and five diagnoses (depression, anxiety and three cardiovascular conditions) recorded at any time during the study, including after the arrest; other drug and alcohol use, socio-economic position and family history were not measured; the listed outcome codes omit the drug-induced psychosis codes that the text says were included; and the authors describe the analysis as exploratory and not preregistered. The hazard ratios rose with the number of arrests (4.49 for one, 6.25 for five or more), but arrests were counted over the whole follow-up and reflect police contact rather than amount of use.

Huang et al. (2022), a Taiwanese registry cohort read in full (ROBINS-E very high on its first-pass card, from confounding), agrees in direction with a much larger estimate (HR 5.28, 4.90–5.70) for a first recorded psychosis diagnosis after a first arrest for an amphetamine-type substance, against insured people with no drug record. It is not counted as inconsistency, because exposure (arrest, with MDMA and other substances pooled with methamphetamine), comparator (no record of any illicit drug use) and outcome (claims diagnoses) differ and the adjustment is minimal: age, sex and five comorbidity codes partly recorded after the arrest, nothing for other drug or alcohol use, socio-economic position or family history. It does not earn an upgrade for large effect, because these remaining biases, and more contact with services after arrest, all run away from the null; nor for dose–response, because its gradient by number of arrests uses arrests counted over the whole follow-up (more arrests go with longer observation) and its printed trend test is reproduced by a regression on five category rates. Its rehabilitation comparison (HR 0.74 for the roughly 10% offered treatment under deferred prosecution, chosen by prosecutors for promising outcomes) is not used. It is an independent sample from a different country and design, so it adds to the replication of the direction, not to the precision of any one estimate.

expect.statement: Among US adults aged 18–64, estimated past-year methamphetamine use rose from about 1.61 million in 2015 to 1.97 million in 2019 (about +22%, editors' calculation) and past-year methamphetamine use disorder (DSM-IV criteria) from about 741,000 to 1.09 million (about +47%, editors' calculation), while overdose deaths involving psychostimulants other than cocaine rose from 5,526 to 15,489 (+180%). More than half of the 2019 deaths also involved opioids, but deaths not involving opioids also rose, from 3,220 to 7,051. The death code (ICD-10 T43.6) covers psychostimulants other than cocaine; the authors report that about 85–90% of such certificates mention methamphetamine. The survey excludes unsheltered and institutionalized people and relies on self-report, so use is probably underestimated. The paper's headline increases for use (43%) and for use disorder without injection (105%) are calculated from 2016, the lowest year, not from 2015. These 2015–2019 figures (ages 18–64, DSM-IV) are not comparable with the 2024 survey figures shown in this section (ages 12 and over, DSM-5). Counting all ages, overdose deaths that a later analysis of the national death records labels methamphetamine-involved (its ICD-10 codes are given only in a supplement, not read) rose from 547 in 1999 to 34,855 in 2023 (crude rate 0.20 to 10.41 per 100,000; 2023 data provisional). The increase averaged 18.5% a year, was steepest in 2018–2021 (37.4% a year) and slowed to 3.4% a year (95% CI 0.2–6.8) in 2021–2023. Deaths involving methamphetamine with fentanyl rose by 76% a year in 2012–2021 and 8.6% a year in 2021–2023, while those with other opioids fell by 27% a year in 2021–2023; no count or share of methamphetamine-involved deaths that also involved opioids is printed (a figure plots their rates, and the overlap of the fentanyl and other-opioid series is not given). The analysis gives two counts for 2023 (34,855 and 35,126), its rates are crude rather than age-adjusted, and its all-ages series is not directly comparable with the 2015–2019 counts for ages 18–64.
expect.plain: In US household surveys of adults aged 18 to 64, the estimated number who said they had used meth in the past year rose by about a fifth between 2015 and 2019, and the number with a meth use disorder by about half; the surveys miss people who are homeless or in institutions. Over the same years, overdose deaths involving stimulants other than cocaine (mostly meth) nearly tripled; more than half of the 2019 deaths also involved opioids, but deaths without opioids also more than doubled. The bigger percentages often quoted from this paper start from 2016, the lowest year. Later US survey figures use different methods and are not directly comparable. Newer death records for all ages show that deaths involving meth kept rising, from about 550 in 1999 to about 35,000 in 2023, but the rise slowed after 2021 (the latest year's figures are provisional). Deaths involving both meth and fentanyl rose fastest. These newer counts come from the same death records and include all ages, so they extend the earlier figures rather than confirm them.
expect.grade.reasoning: Repeated national survey (NSDUH) and death-certificate counts; observational, starts low (§6.3). Not upgraded: large effect concerns the size of an exposure's effect under adjustment, not a change in counts over time (§6.3, descriptive claims), and the survey trends (+22% use, +47% use disorder; intervals overlapping between 2015 and 2019; trend tests significant) are not large. Risk of bias not downgraded for the trend (JBI moderate): the frame excludes unsheltered and institutionalized people and about half of sampled people completed an interview, which lowers the levels more than it changes the trend. The death series is a code (ICD-10 T43.6), about 85–90% of whose certificates mention methamphetamine, and about 6% of 2019 overdose certificates named no drug, so the counts are a proxy and an undercount. The all-ages extension to 2023 (Zhu et al., 2025; JBI moderate on its study card) draws on the same national death records, so it extends the series rather than replicating it (status stays single-study); its codes are not shown in the article, 2023 data are provisional, two different 2023 counts are given and two subgroup averages in its table appear transposed. These faults affect exact figures, not the direction of the rise or the timing of the slowdown after 2021, so the rating is not downgraded; the 2021–2023 slowdown is a segment fitted to three yearly values, the last of them provisional. A CDC report on overdose deaths involving stimulants, January 2018 to June 2024 (Tanz et al., 2025), has not yet been read.

expect.statement: In the studies that compared group means with population norms, average test scores of people with methamphetamine dependence mostly fell in the low-average to average range: between the 16th and 55th percentiles after about 6 days of verified abstinence in one study, whose authors set the impaired range at the 2nd percentile or below. A group mean in the normal range does not show that every individual is, nor does it exclude a decline from a higher starting point, which no study measured. One review disputes reading normed scores as a categorical line, arguing that mild deficits can still matter, and cites initial evidence of lower scores on performance measures of everyday functioning (Dean et al., 2013). A minority met impairment criteria, more often than controls: about 7 of 27 people who used methamphetamine versus 2 of 18 controls met a 2-SD criterion in at least one domain in one study (as summarized, with ambiguous wording, in a review; for working memory alone, 1 versus 2; the primary paper is still to be read), and 34% of the methamphetamine group versus 16% of controls had a global deficit score above 0.5 in another (a cut-off the authors equate with roughly the 16th percentile and describe as relatively liberal, though validated and widely used), in which only the group that kept using differed significantly (38%; abstainers 24%), more than half of the methamphetamine group but no controls had HIV, and controls were also screened free of hepatitis C, ADHD and antisocial personality disorder.
expect.plain: In the studies that compared them with test norms, groups of people dependent on meth scored on average in the low-average to average range, not in the range the authors called impaired. An average in the normal range does not mean every person is, and it cannot show whether someone's scores dropped from a higher starting point, because no one was tested before. One review argues that even a small drop within the normal range can matter, pointing to early evidence of lower scores on tests of everyday tasks. In two studies that counted individuals, about a quarter to a third of people who used meth met a definition of impairment, compared with about one in nine to one in six people who didn't. The two studies drew the line differently: one counted very low scores (about the bottom 2%) in any one area, the other an overall score in roughly the bottom sixth. In one of them, more than half of the people who used meth had HIV and none of the comparison group did, which could explain part of that difference.
expect.magnitude: Group means between about the 16th and 55th percentiles on normed tests (Simon et al., 2010); impaired in at least one domain 7/27 (26%) vs 2/18 (11%) (Kalechstein et al., 2003, as reported by Hart et al., 2012); globally impaired 34% vs 16% (Iudicello et al., 2010).
expect.grade.reasoning: Observational, starts low. Risk of bias: different impairment definitions and norm sets; group means compared with norms without demographic matching; in the impairment-rate study, HIV, hepatitis C, ADHD and antisocial personality disorder present only in people who used methamphetamine. Imprecision: the proportions come from samples of 27 vs 18 and 83 vs 38. Status replicated for group means; the higher impairment rate in people who used methamphetamine rests on two studies, one reported second-hand and one confounded by HIV.

nor does it exclude a decline from a higher starting point. No study tested people before they began to use. One study from the same laboratory as the percentile study (Dean et al., 2018; 37 people with methamphetamine dependence after about a week of abstinence, 41 controls) predicted each person's adult score from school grades before first use, parental income, age and smoking, with a model fitted in the controls that explained about 40% of their variance: the methamphetamine group's grades before first use were already lower (grade point average 2.1 against 2.5), and their adult scores fell below the prediction (overall, a standardized paired difference of 0.61; attention 0.69, memory 0.46; executive function not below). These scores were standardized to the controls, not to population norms, the model's own uncertainty was not carried into the tests, and other substance use disorders were far more common in the methamphetamine group.

(2018; ROBINS-E high on its first-pass card), from the same laboratory as Simon et al. (2010) and the review by Dean et al. (2013), qualifies the caveat that no starting point was measured: it estimates one from school grades before first use, a proxy rather than a pre-use test, with a prediction model fitted in 41 controls that explains about 40% of the variance and whose uncertainty the paired tests ignore, scores standardized to the controls rather than to norms, testing after about a week of abstinence, and far more other substance use disorders in the methamphetamine group. It bears on whether scores fell from a higher starting point, not on whether group means lie within norms, so it changes neither the rating nor the status.

evidence_add.extracted: 37 non-treatment-seeking adults with methamphetamine dependence, tested after a mean of 6.9 days of urine-verified abstinence, and 41 healthy controls of similar age, education and estimated IQ. Grade point average from school transcripts for years before self-reported first use: 2.1 (SD 0.7) vs 2.5 (0.6), p = 0.016. A regression fitted in the controls (adult composite on age, parental income, smoking status and grade point average; R² 0.41) predicted higher scores than the methamphetamine group obtained: overall d 0.61, t(36) = 3.732, p = 0.001; attention/concentration 0.69 (p < 0.001), memory 0.46 (p < 0.01), executive function not lower (p = 0.87). The d values equal t/√37, a paired standardized difference (editors' check).

evidence_add.extracted: Scores were standardized to the control group, not to published norms. The shortfall remained with withdrawal partialled out (d 0.54, p = 0.002), with standardized school test scores in place of grades (24 and 19 participants; d 1.41) and in grade-matched subgroups of 28 (d 0.71). Lifetime alcohol, cocaine, marijuana and other drug abuse or dependence: 26, 12, 21 and 9 of 37 in the methamphetamine group vs 9, 0, 9 and 0 of 41 controls. The authors state that effects of methamphetamine cannot be disentangled from other drug use, that the methods do not show a causal relationship, that the predictors explain about 40% of the variance, and that the control sample was modest for prediction.
